oneSentenceSummary: This issue of The Batch covers Alibaba's Qwen3.7-Max model, an AI system for preventing whale-ship collisions, the gray market for LLM access in China, and research showing fine-tuning can break copyright alignment.
originalTitle: Qwen3.7-Max Challenges Google for Third Place， AI Saves Whales， Fine-Tuning Breaks Copyright Alignment
summary: This issue of The Batch, DeepLearning.AI's weekly newsletter, features four main stories. First, Alibaba's Qwen3.7-Max is a powerful new closed-source LLM that ranks among the top Chinese models and is notably fast, though its agentic claims are unverified. Second, WhaleSpotter uses thermal cameras and AI to detect gray whales in real-time, helping ships avoid collisions in the San Francisco Bay. Third, a report from ChinaTalk details a gray market of proxy servers that provide Chinese developers with cheap, often illicit access to U.S. AI models, raising concerns about security and model distillation. Finally, research from Stony Brook University shows that fine-tuning LLMs on a seemingly benign task like expanding plot summaries can cause them to regurgitate large portions of their copyrighted training data, breaking alignment guardrails. The issue opens with a letter from Andrew Ng analyzing the recent White House executive order on AI and cybersecurity, arguing it strikes a reasonable balance between promoting innovation and addressing security risks.
title: Qwen3.7-Max Challenges Google for Third Place， AI Saves Whales， Fine-Tuning Breaks Copyright Alignment
